name: Format Factory
tagline: Windows desktop media converter that turns video, audio, image and disc files into other formats.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. The free build is the one most people use.

verdictSummary: Format Factory is a graphical wrapper around codec libraries that already live on your machine for free. FFmpeg does essentially all of the conversion work, and an agent can wrap it in a drag-and-drop local app in a single session. There is no account, no sync, no network, nothing to lose except the preset list and the installer convenience. The honest caveat: you are trading a tested GUI for your own, and you will discover the long tail of weird codecs yourself. For the eighty percent case of 'make this MKV an MP4' the DIY build is done before the download finishes.
coreLoopDIY: A local drag-and-drop app that queues files, runs FFmpeg with named presets, and writes the converted output next to the originals or to a chosen folder.
requirements: FFmpeg and FFprobe installed and on PATH
Desktop OS with a browser or Electron runtime
whatYouLose: Dozens of curated presets for devices and formats nobody remembers
DVD and disc ripping paths that involve more than FFmpeg
A tested GUI with progress, pause, error recovery and batch retry
Image and document format handling bundled into the same tool
An installer that a non-technical relative can actually use
moatNotes: The moat is the preset library and the fact that it already installs in one click. Both are convenience, not defensibility.
whyPeopleStillPay: Mostly they do not, since the main product is free and monetized around the edges. The people who stay are the ones who want a window with buttons rather than a terminal, and who converted a file once in 2011 and never needed to learn anything else. That is real value, it just is not value an agent cannot reproduce in an afternoon.
notes: This is a GUI on top of free codecs, which makes it the most one-shottable category of desktop software there is.
prompt:
Build a local desktop media converter called Hopper. Single folder, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Node.js 20 with Electron for the shell
- Plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JS for the UI, no framework
- FFmpeg and FFprobe invoked as child processes from PATH, do not bundle binaries
- better-sqlite3 for a tiny local job history database in the app data folder

What it does:
1. Window with a large drop zone. Dropping files or folders queues every media file found, recursing one level.
2. For each queued file, run ffprobe and show container, duration, video codec, audio codec, resolution and size.
3. A preset picker with exactly these presets: MP4 H264 AAC, MP4 H265 AAC, WebM VP9 Opus, MP3 192k, WAV 16 bit, GIF 480p 12fps, Audio extract copy, Fast remux to MP4. Each preset is a named object with an argv array, defined in one file called presets.js so a user can add their own.
4. Output settings: target folder (default is next to source), filename suffix, overwrite toggle.
5. Convert All runs jobs with a configurable concurrency, default 2. Parse ffmpeg stderr for the time= field and render a per file progress bar plus overall progress.
6. Per job: cancel, retry, reveal in file manager, and a button to copy the exact ffmpeg command that was run.
7. Failed jobs stay in the list with the last 20 lines of stderr viewable inline.
8. Job history persisted in SQLite, with a history view and a clear history button.

Explicitly out of scope: DVD and Blu-ray ripping, DRM, image format conversion, subtitle editing, GPU encoder auto detection, any update checker, any network request at all.

If FFmpeg is missing on launch, show a blocking screen with install instructions per OS and a recheck button.

No secrets needed, so no .env. Ship a README with run, build and packaging steps for macOS, Windows and Linux.
